Your template is already doing the right things for Apple Mail — `<meta name="color-scheme" content="dark">`, `supported-color-schemes`, inline `color-scheme:dark` on `<html>`, and explicit dark backgrounds on every element. With those declarations, iPhone's **Apple Mail** should leave the email dark and untouched.

So the question is which app you saw it in — and given we were just testing BIMI there, I suspect the **Gmail app on iPhone**. That changes everything: Gmail's app dark mode ignores all color-scheme declarations and applies its own luminance-based recolor to the email body — and it's notorious for flipping *already-dark* designs to light (it re-maps colors toward its own theme rather than preserving yours). The comment in our renderer ("clients invert light emails, never dark ones") holds for Apple Mail but is unfortunately false for the Gmail app. There is **no opt-out** — no header, meta, or CSS reliably stops it; the known blend-mode double-inversion hack doesn't survive Gmail's mobile apps either.

Realistic options:

1. **Confirm the split first**: open the same email in Apple Mail on the iPhone. If it's dark there and light in Gmail's app, everything is working as well as email allows, and this is purely Gmail-app behavior every dark-design sender lives with.
2. **Make the inverted version presentable** instead of fighting it: I can render one of our emails, simulate Gmail's approximate luminance flip on the palette, and tune the handful of tokens (borders, muted text, button) whose inverted forms look worst — so the Gmail-app rendering degrades into a passable "light theme" instead of a broken one. The dark banner images will stay dark either way, which is the main visual clash.
3. **The nuclear option** — ship light-themed emails and let clients darken them — would betray the brand and make Apple Mail worse, so I'd rule it out.

If Apple Mail on your iPhone is showing it light too, that's a genuine surprise — tell me and I'll pull the exact rendered HTML apart, because then something in our output is defeating the declarations.

interface DripItem {
  id: string;
  body: string;
  position: string;
  title: string;
  url: string;
  image: string;
}

const items: DripItem[] = allPosts
  .filter((post) => !post.private && post.image)
  .map((post) => ({
    id: post.slug,
    body: post.title,
    position: '',
    title: post.title,
    url: post.url,
    image: post.image,
  }));

const ADVANCE_EVERY_MS = 4500;

const root = ref<HTMLElement | null>(null);
const scroller = ref<HorizontalScrollerNs.Exposed<DripItem> | null>(null);
const arrivingId = ref('');
// everything at or left of this index has been delivered — those cards
// wear the checkmark; the arriving card gets the full stamp first
const deliveredThrough = ref(-1);

let timer: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | undefined;
let arrivingTimer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
let observer: IntersectionObserver | undefined;
let inView = false;
let hovering = false;
let current = 0;

/** The card resting under the strip's center — read from the scroller's
 *  OWN geometry (position + half the container), never estimated from
 *  CSS. With snap-align="center" this is also the card every step
 *  centers, so "the arriving card" is a guarantee, not a guess. */
function centerIndexAtRest(): number {
  const scrollerInstance = scroller.value;
  if (!scrollerInstance) return 0;
  const position =
    parseFloat(String(scrollerInstance.scrollPosition)) || 0;
  return (
    scrollerInstance.getIndexAtPosition(
      position + scrollerInstance.containerOuterSize / 2,
    )?.index ?? 0
  );
}

/** One delivery: the stamp plays on card `index`, then settles into its
 *  permanent checkmark by advancing the frontier. */
function deliver(index: number) {
  arrivingId.value = items[index]?.id ?? '';
  clearTimeout(arrivingTimer);
  arrivingTimer = setTimeout(() => {
    arrivingId.value = '';
    deliveredThrough.value = Math.max(deliveredThrough.value, index);
  }, 2600);
}

/** Load AND wrap start identically: the clamped cards left of center are
 *  HISTORY (checked, no stamp — like older mail already in the inbox);
 *  the centered card is the first to actually arrive. Every later check
 *  is therefore preceded by that card's own stamp. */
function beginCycle() {
  current = centerIndexAtRest();
  deliveredThrough.value = current - 1;
  // snap the opening card onto the exact center — the stamp rides it
  scroller.value?.scrollToIndex(current);
  deliver(current);
}

function advance() {
  const scrollerInstance = scroller.value;
  if (!scrollerInstance || !inView || hovering || document.hidden) return;
  if (scrollerInstance.lenis?.isScrolling) return; // the reader owns it
  if (current >= items.length - 1) {
    // the loop wrapped — reset to the start and begin a fresh cycle
    deliveredThrough.value = -1;
    scrollerInstance.scrollToIndex(0, () => beginCycle(), true, 0);
    return;
  }
  current += 1;
  scrollerInstance.scrollToIndex(current, () => deliver(current));
}

onMounted(() => {
  if (window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches) return;
  if (items.length < 2) return;
  observer = new IntersectionObserver(
    ([entry]) => {
      inView = entry.isIntersecting;
    },
    { threshold: 0.35 },
  );
  if (root.value) observer.observe(root.value);
  // first cycle after the strip has measured its opening cards
  setTimeout(() => beginCycle(), 600);
  timer = setInterval(advance, ADVANCE_EVERY_MS);
});

onBeforeUnmount(() => {
  if (timer) clearInterval(timer);
  clearTimeout(arrivingTimer);
  observer?.disconnect();
});

Quick correction to the premise first: today the emails don't word-wrap — the `<pre>` keeps shiki's `white-space: pre` plus our `overflow-x: auto`, so long lines scroll where the client honors overflow and *clip* where it doesn't. That's what you can see in the screenshot I posted earlier: the `// plain getter — derives on rea…` comment is cut at the card edge.

Here's the real decision landscape:

**Horizontal scroll** works beautifully in exactly one place: Apple Mail (WebKit honors `overflow-x` on the pre). Gmail — desktop webmail is inconsistent about overflow, and the Gmail mobile apps largely strip it. And Gmail mobile is precisely the audience we just built the light variant for. Where overflow is stripped, the failure mode is nasty: the unwrapped line either clips silently (reader loses the end of the line and doesn't know it) or forces the *whole email* wider than the viewport, so the entire message pans sideways. There's also a UX point independent of support: horizontal panning inside an email fights the mail app's own gestures — even where it works, almost nobody discovers it.

**Word wrap** (`white-space: pre-wrap`) is the boring universal answer: every client renders it, nothing is ever hidden, nothing stretches the layout. The cost is aesthetic — a wrapped code line with a hanging continuation looks less like an editor. In our specific case the cost is small: the email column fits roughly 65 characters of 12.5px mono, and the posts' code is authored to ~70ch (the ivue skill style keeps lines short), so only the occasional long comment or template literal wraps, by a word or two.

My recommendation: **wrap, and keep the scroll as a progressive enhancement** — set `white-space: pre-wrap; word-break: break-word` on the pre and drop `overflow-x`. A hybrid ("scroll where supported, wrap elsewhere") isn't really achievable: you can't feature-detect inside static email HTML, and the two properties contradict on the same element. So it's genuinely either/or, and "every reader sees all the code" beats "Apple Mail readers see prettier code while Gmail readers lose line ends."

One refinement that softens the aesthetic cost: wrapping only matters at the margin, so we could also nudge the email code font down half a pixel (12.5 → 12) buying ~3 extra characters per line — most lines then never wrap at all.
